newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Asia oil body would avert supply shocks.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Asia oil body would avert supply shocks.

text.p: Asia's booming demand for oil could cause major supply problems in the years to come, an influential Japanese business group pushing for a sub-APEC oil group says.

The Keizai Doyukai, or Japan Association of Corporate Executives, unveiled a detailed proposal earlier this month after calling in May for the establishment of an Asian oil organization to deal with supply security issues and manage energy relations with the Middle East.

The Doyukai proposal called for the creation of medium- to long-term strategic oil storage facilities to be shared by Asian countries, collaboration in oil refining ventures and the collection of regional energy statistics.
"The basic supply and demand situation in Asia is really quite serious," said Ariyoshi Okumura, who conceived the plan.
A former chairman of Doyukai's committee on Middle East-Japan relations, Okumura is also a former managing director at the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd.

"The Asia-Pacific region is consuming oil from outside the region at a rate of 10 million barrels per day (bpd). If you are a believer in linear extrapolation, we will need 20 million bpd by 2010," Okumura said.
"While I find that projection questionable, it is a certainty that energy shortages in Asia will be a serious concern for our governments in the years to come," he added.
The group's proposal calls for the formation of a Tokyo-based oil body that would operate under the auspices of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
The organiaation, to be named the Asia-Pacific Organisation for Energy Dialogue (APOED), would provide Asian countries a forum in which to coordinate their energy needs.
"Many governments in Asia do not publish any kind of detailed energy statistics," Okumura said.

"In order to cope with any emergency supply disruptions, the Asia Pacific has to have significant stockpiles. Japan has a substantial stockpile, but we don't know anything about China, nor do we know about the strategic reserves of Indonesia, South Korea, Singapore and Malaysia," he said.
Okumura says the proposal is still being considered by APEC, adding: "APEC should be a very appropriate organisation to provide an umbrella for this initiative."
He added that more contact was needed with oil-producing countries.
"We have to broaden the base of human contact with the Middle East and Central Asia. That's the only way for Japan to have energy security, economic security," he added.
Okumura said he hoped to see the oil body set up within three years.
"Five years is too long, but one is too short because so many governments are involved," Okumura said.
The APOED proposal notes that Japan's target of reducing the oil portion of its energy needs to 50 percent by 2010 has become unrealistic because of delays in nuclear power development.
